```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Class enumeration estimates one mixture model for each number of classes.
Each model is fitted from its own starting values, and the numbering of its
classes is arbitrary, so class 2 of a three-class solution has no defined
relation to class 2 of a four-class solution. The relation between two
solutions is carried by the observations they classify. When the classes of
the larger solution subdivide those of the smaller one, each class of the
smaller solution passes its members to one or more classes of the larger,
and the solutions are nested. When the larger solution redistributes
observations across class boundaries, the classes of the two solutions
overlap without nesting. A clustering tree represents these relations for a
sequence of solutions (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). Each row of the tree is
one solution, divided into its classes in proportion to their size, and the
band between two classes in adjacent rows is proportional to the
observations they share.

In a mixture model each observation belongs to every class with a posterior
probability. For two solutions $A$ and $B$ fitted to the same $N$
observations, with posterior probabilities $p_{ia}$ and $q_{ib}$ and
observation weights $w_i$, the shared posterior mass of class $a$ of $A$ and
class $b$ of $B$ is

$$m_{ab} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, p_{ia} \, q_{ib}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}.$$

The masses form a joint distribution over the pairs of classes. Summed over
the classes of $B$, they give the posterior share of class $a$, and summed
over the classes of $A$, the posterior share of class $b$. The ratio of
$m_{ab}$ to the share of $a$ is the part of class $a$ that the larger
solution places in class $b$. A tree built from posterior probabilities
retains the uncertainty of the classification, which a tree built from
modal assignments discards.

A two-level mixture model has two sequences of solutions (Vermunt, 2003).
Observations are classified into classes, and the groups that contain them
are classified into group classes by their distribution over those classes.
The classes form a tree at each number of group classes, and the group
classes form a tree at each number of classes. Solutions can also be
compared at a single level, for example the four-class solutions estimated
with different numbers of group classes, whose classes need not coincide.

## Data and candidates

`student_esm` holds experience-sampling data from 100 university students
(Neubauer and Schmiedek, 2024). At each prompt when they had not studied
since the previous one, the students reported which of eight leisure
activities they had done. The prompts are the observations and the students
the groups. The candidates combine one to six classes of prompts with one to
four group classes of students.

```{r candidates, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(latents)
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            categorical = activities, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
```

```{r candidates-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_failed <- with(candidates, sum(!converged %in% TRUE))
```

The grid holds `r n_candidates` candidates. Their classes of prompts are
counted by `n_profiles`, the name the package uses at both levels of a
two-level model. The `r n_failed` candidates with one class and several group
classes could not be estimated. A group class is defined by its distribution
over the classes, and with a single class every group has the same
distribution. Every tree with two or more group classes therefore begins at
two classes.

## The tree at one number of group classes

At one group class the model is a single-level latent class model of the
prompts. Its tree shows how the classes of prompts divide as classes are
added.

```{r tree-one, fig.height = 5}
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)
```

```{r tree-one-values, include = FALSE}
splits <- get_results(models, "tree", n_group_classes = 1)
two_to_three <- subset(splits, from_candidate == "classes2_groups1")
media_kept <- with(subset(two_to_three, from_share > 0.5), max(share_of_from))
offline_kept <- with(subset(two_to_three, from_share < 0.5), max(share_of_from))
offline_to_media <- with(subset(two_to_three, from_share < 0.5 & to_share > 0.5),
                         share_of_from)
three_to_four <- subset(splits, from_candidate == "classes3_groups1")
job_share <- with(three_to_four, min(from_share))
job_kept <- with(subset(three_to_four, from_share < 0.1), max(share_of_from))
# The classes the text names, pinned by their own numbers.
smallest <- subset(three_to_four, from_share == job_share)
job_class <- with(smallest, unique(from_class))
yes_three <- subset(get_results(get_candidate(models, n_profiles = 3,
                                              n_group_classes = 1), "responses"),
                    category == "yes")
job_probability <- with(subset(yes_three, indicator == "part_time_job" &
                                 profile == job_class), probability)
media_class <- with(subset(two_to_three, from_share > 0.5), unique(from_class))
yes_two <- subset(get_results(get_candidate(models, n_profiles = 2,
                                            n_group_classes = 1), "responses"),
                  category == "yes" & indicator == "on_social_media")
media_probability <- with(subset(yes_two, profile == media_class), probability)
offline_probability <- with(subset(yes_two, profile != media_class), probability)
# The text below names these classes; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(media_kept > 0.7, offline_kept > 0.6, job_share < 0.1,
          job_kept > 0.9, length(job_class) == 1L, job_probability > 0.9,
          media_probability > offline_probability)
```

```{r responses-three, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_responses(get_candidate(models, n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 1),
               intervals = FALSE)
```

The two-class solution separates prompts with media use (social media,
television or games, music) from prompts with offline activities. In the
three-class solution the media class keeps
`r round(100 * media_kept)`% of its posterior mass. The offline class divides
into three parts. The largest, `r round(100 * offline_kept)`%, forms a class
of time with friends and walking, `r round(100 * offline_to_media)`% joins the
media class, and the remainder forms a class of `r round(100 * job_share)`% of
prompts in which the probability of a part-time job is
`r sprintf("%.2f", job_probability)`. The part-time job class passes
`r round(100 * job_kept)`% of its mass to a single class of the four-class
solution, so it persists as further classes are added.

## Every tree

Without a choice of group classes, each number of group classes has its own
tree, returned as a separate plot. On an interactive screen device the plots
are shown one at a time.

```{r trees, fig.height = 5}
plot_tree(models)
```

A later tree matches its classes to those of the first tree using a one-to-one
assignment of posterior overlap at the same number of classes. The assignment
maximizes total overlap for square matches up to eight classes; larger or
rectangular matches use a greedy assignment. A class can therefore be matched
to something other than its own largest-overlap class. Colours mark these
assigned correspondences. `combine = TRUE` plots
every tree as a panel of one figure.

## Comparing solutions at one level

A single value of `n_profiles` selects one level of every tree. The rows of
the plot are then the solutions with that number of classes, one for each
number of group classes, and the bands show where the same prompts are
classified in each.

```{r level, fig.height = 3}
plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))
```

The values behind the plot are returned by `get_results()` with the same
arguments, one row per pair of classes.

```{r level-table}
get_results(models, "tree", n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))
```

```{r level-values, include = FALSE}
compared <- get_results(models, "tree", n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))
retained <- aggregate(share_of_from ~ from_class, compared, max)
retained_low <- with(retained, min(share_of_from))
retained_high <- with(retained, max(share_of_from))
```

Each class of the four-class solution with one group class places between
`r round(100 * retained_low)`% and `r round(100 * retained_high)`% of its
posterior mass in a single class of the solution with three group classes.
The two solutions describe similar classes, and the group classes shift a
part of the prompts between them. Omitting `n_group_classes` compares the
same level across every number of group classes.

```{r level-all, fig.height = 5}
plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4)
```

## Comparing two solutions

Any two candidates are compared with `from` and `to`, each given by its
number of classes and number of group classes.

```{r from-to, fig.height = 3}
plot_tree(models, from = c(3, 1), to = c(4, 3))
```

The candidates can also be given by name, in the order of the rows, with
`candidates = c("classes3_groups1", "classes4_groups3")`.

## The tree of group classes

With `level = "groups"` the units are the students and the classes are the
group classes. A tree then runs down the numbers of group classes at one
number of classes of prompts.

```{r groups, fig.height = 4}
plot_tree(models, level = "groups", n_profiles = 4)
```

```{r groups-values, include = FALSE}
group_splits <- get_results(models, "tree", level = "groups", n_profiles = 4)
two_to_three_groups <- subset(group_splits, from_candidate == "classes4_groups2")
group_kept <- with(two_to_three_groups, max(share_of_to))
```

From two to three group classes, one group class of the three-group-class
solution receives `r round(100 * group_kept)`% of its students from a single
group class of the two-group-class solution. The other group classes draw
their students from both. The tree of group classes is read in the same way
as the tree of classes. With `level = "groups"`, a single value of
`n_group_classes` compares one level of group classes across numbers of
classes, as `n_profiles` does for the classes.

## Summary of calls

| Question | Call |
|---|---|
| How do the classes divide as classes are added? | `plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)` |
| The same for every number of group classes | `plot_tree(models)`, `combine = TRUE` for one figure |
| How do the solutions with four classes differ across group classes? | `plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))` |
| How do two chosen solutions correspond? | `plot_tree(models, from = c(3, 1), to = c(4, 3))` |
| How do the group classes divide? | `plot_tree(models, level = "groups", n_profiles = 4)` |
| The shared masses behind any of these | `get_results(models, "tree", ...)` with the same arguments |

```{r restore, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```

## References

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on
multiple time scales. *Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27*(1),
147-168. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8>

Vermunt, J. K. (2003). Multilevel latent class models. *Sociological
Methodology*, 33, 213--239.

Zappia, L., & Oshlack, A. (2018). Clustering trees: A visualization for
evaluating clusterings at multiple resolutions. *GigaScience*, 7(7),
giy083.
